## Discontinuation of GENERATION HD2 (tominersen) and POINT-HD (RG6496)

Posted on July 10, 2026 by Lisanne Walter

On Thursday 9 July 2026, Roche announced the discontinuation of two EHDN-endorsed studies:

• GENERATION HD2 (clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05686551): A phase 2/open-label extension study of tominersen compared with placebo in Huntington’s disease (HD).
• POINT-HD (clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07246941): A phase 1 study of RG6496 delivered intrathecally compared with placebo in HD.

The community letter from Roche can be read in full here.

We share the disappointment of the HD community and will shortly issue a full statement from the EHDN Executive Committee via our usual channels.

We remain grateful for the unwavering generosity and commitment of the HD community to taking part in research and, in doing so, advancing our understanding of HD.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On 9ᵗʰ July 2026, Roche announced the discontinuation of the GENERATION HD2 (NCT05686551)²² study of tominersen in people with prodromal and early Huntington’s disease. GENERATION HD2 was initiated following exploratory analyses of the phase III GENERATION HD1 study, which suggested that younger participants with lower disease burden might derive benefit from lower-dose, less frequent administration of tominersen.⁴⁴ After completion of the planned 16-month treatment period in all 301 participants, top-line analyses showed that tominersen was well tolerated and achieved significant reductions in mHTT protein and NFL concentrations compared with placebo. However, these biomarker effects did not translate into a meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes, and Roche therefore discontinued further clinical development of tominersen.²³ Although disappointing for participants and the HD community, these findings still provide important insights for the field. GENERATION HD2 confirms that sustained lowering of mHTT in humans, even if it lowers wild-type as well, and does not trigger HTT exon 1, is associated with robust NFL lowering – often taken as indicating reduced rates of neuronal damage – but that clinical benefits, if they are to emerge, may take longer than 16 months. The study therefore reinforces, rather than resolves, key questions surrounding the therapeutic window, magnitude, duration, molecular target and anatomical distribution of HTT-lowering required to modify disease progression. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Tominersen (RG6042)

Roche / Genentech ↗

3

Evidence entries

1

Clinical trials

Overview

Treatment Details

Mechanism of Action

An antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) delivered by intrathecal injection that binds HTT mRNA and triggers its degradation, reducing production of both mutant and normal huntingtin protein non-selectively. After an earlier Phase 3 trial (GENERATION HD1) was halted for lack of benefit at the studied dose/frequency, Roche then tested a lower, less frequent regimen in people at an earlier stage in the Phase 2 GENERATION HD2 trial. On July 9, 2026, Roche and Genentech discontinued tominersen after that trial lowered mutant huntingtin but did not show clinical benefit.

Dosing Notes

Development was discontinued on July 9, 2026. It was given by intrathecal (spinal) injection every 16 weeks at 60 mg or 100 mg in GENERATION HD2. Not approved and no longer being developed.

## Roche’s decision to discontinue the Ionis-partnered trials came soon after the biotech sustained a late-stage failure in ATTR-CM.

Roche has discontinued two Huntington’s disease studies for investigational antisense therapies being developed in collaboration with Ionis Pharmaceuticals.

The pharma will no longer push through with the Phase 2 GENERATION HD2 study after the embattled asset tominersen failed to meet its key efficacy objective, Roche said in a Thursday letter to the Huntington’s disease community. Meanwhile, a separate clinical trial evaluating a candidate called RG6496 was stopped based on new data from a parallel animal study.

LEXEO therapeutics

Dear Batten disease community,

We are writing to provide an update on Lexeo’s CLN2 disease gene therapy program.

As you may know, Lexeo conducted a Phase 1 study testing the investigational gene therapy, AAVrh10CLN2*, using the intraparenchymal (IPC) route of administration (i.e. direct to brain only). Initial results from this study showed that although AAVrh10CLN2 may have some impact on disease progression, the IPC administration may not be the most optimal route to distribute the therapy throughout the central nervous system.

A new study in monkeys testing the intracisternal magna (ICM) route of administration (i.e. into the cerebrospinal fluid) was also conducted, with results demonstrating improved distribution, indicating that ICM could be a potential alternative to IPC administration.

Lexeo met with FDA following the conclusion of these studies. During this meeting, the agency determined that multiple new animal studies would be required before proceeding further with clinical trials in humans, given ongoing discussion around the route of administration for the gene therapy. These new studies would require additional financial investment and resources.

Following the feedback from this meeting, Lexeo is looking to identify strategic partners or alternatives to help take the CLN2 program forward into additional clinical trials.

We are sharing this information with you as part of our commitment to ongoing, open communication with the community and we recognize that this news will have an impact on families in the Batten disease community. We hope to share more information with you if there are new developments with this program.

If you have any further questions, please reach out to: clinicaltrials@lexeotx.com

Sincerely,  
The Lexeo Team

Questions & Answers

**What did the analysis results show?**  
The iDMC conducted the interim analysis and Roche does not have access to the data reviewed. We are modifying the GENERATION HD2 study based on the iDMC’s recommendations, which were to continue the study and to switch participants on the 60mg dose to the 100mg dose.

**Does this mean that the 60mg dose did not work or was not safe?**  
The iDMC reviewed available trial data and did not raise any concerns regarding participant safety or signs of symptoms worsening with either tominersen dose. Roche is changing the GENERATION HD2 study design to only test the 100mg dose against placebo for the remainder of the study. This change is based on the iDMC’s recommendation that the 100mg dose was more likely than the 60mg dose to result in clinical benefit for people with HD.

**Does this mean that the 100mg dose works?**  
The iDMC recommended that the 100mg dose should continue to be tested in the study, based on their review of interim data. The GENERATION HD2 study is ongoing and we cannot draw final conclusions at this time. The study is expected to complete in 2026.

**Will study participants know which dose they were receiving? What does “blinding” mean?**  
From the start of the study, participants, study teams and Roche do not know treatment assignments. This is called “blinding” and it is done to avoid bias in how the study is run and results are obtained. When the study is “unblinded” after the end of the study, it will be possible for participants to learn which treatment group they were assigned - tominersen (including the dose) or placebo.

**What happens now for study participants?**  
All participants will be contacted by their study sites and asked to consent to continue in the modified study. There will be no change to any participants’ overall study experience or schedules. After consent, the study pharmacy will switch the dosing of participants previously assigned the 60mg dose to the 100mg dose. There will be no change for participants previously assigned the 100mg and placebo groups. Treatment assignments remain “blinded” to participants, sites and Roche.
